positions.text: Hu, Rong, and Van Kleek sharpen Kaal's claim that iterability must be engineered. Their FAccT 2026 analysis identifies persistent identity, repeated interaction, retained histories, and sanction-sensitive future consequences as necessary preconditions for reputation; it then argues that present language-model agents do not supply those properties intrinsically and require ex ante protocol-based behavioral harnesses. This independently supports the institutional-design premise that iterability is constructed, while qualifying Kaal's implementation: ex post identity-based reputation remains unsafe unless the protocol first solves agent dissociation and configuration continuity.
scope_conditions: The response is limited to the full-text passages and the one mapped Kaal claim.
External evidence level: published FAccT 2026 proceedings article with public arXiv v3 full text, ACM DOI, and independent Crossref/OpenAlex identity, publication, and non-retraction checks.
Mapping review tier: independent substantive scholarly-growth qualification.
The retained paper is an institutional and jurisprudential argument, not an empirical implementation test of Kaal's substrate.

It contests identity-based ex post reputation for currently dissociative language-model agents and favors ex ante protocol harnesses; the relationship therefore qualifies rather than generally validates Kaal's design.
The paper does not test Kaal's staking, validation-pool, settlement, reputation-decay, or capability-tag mechanisms.

Its persistent-identity and iteration preconditions support the engineered-iterability premise only when configuration continuity, memory, attribution, and sanction sensitivity are actually supplied by protocol.

sourceEvidencePassages.text: Reputation systems do not merely record past behavior. They are also sanctioning institutions that operate as social corrective feedback loops [20], presupposing a particular kind of subject: one whose identity persists, whose past behavior has predictive relevance, whose memory carries consequences forward, whose reputation is costly to abandon, and whose sanctions alter future conduct.
C1—Persistent identity. The rated entity must persist across time so that past ratings apply to future interactions.

locator.section: 2.2 Eight Preconditions That Reputation Mechanisms Depend On

sourceEvidencePassages.text: C3—Iteration. The same entities must interact repeatedly, creating Axelrod’s “shadow of the future” [9]. If the agent is replaced between rounds, there is no shadow and no reason to invest in reputation; the discount factor in reputation games encodes exactly this value of continued interaction [55].

locator.section: 2.2 Eight Preconditions That Reputation Mechanisms Depend On

sourceEvidencePassages.text: We argue that identity-based, ex post, sanction-based governance such as reputation is structurally inapplicable to dissociative agents, and that governance should shift to observability-based, ex ante, protocol-based behavioral harnesses.

locator.section: 5.3 From Ex Post Governance to Ex Ante Harnesses
